title: Stationary Drop Punt
objective: Develop a technically sound stationary drop punt by teaching correct ball drop, body position, foot contact and follow-through before introducing movement or defensive pressure.
players:
Minimum: 2
Ideal: 10–20
Maximum: Unlimited (working in pairs)
setup:
Players work in pairs facing each other.
Players should stand:
Under 8–10: 8–10 metres apart.
Under 12–14: 10–15 metres apart.
Under 16 and above: 15–20 metres apart.
Spread pairs evenly across the training area to prevent footballs crossing into neighbouring groups.
howTheDrillWorks:
Player A begins with the football.
Player A performs a stationary drop punt to Player B.
Player B marks or gathers the football.
Player B resets before returning the kick.
Continue for the nominated time.
Swap the preferred kicking foot after several minutes if appropriate.
Players should prioritise correct technique rather than kicking distance.
coachingPoints: Focus on one coaching point at a time.
Guide the ball onto the boot rather than throwing it.
Keep their head over the football.
Strike the ball with the laces of the boot.
Follow through directly towards the target.
Encourage smooth, controlled kicking rather than maximum power.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Provide one coaching correction before allowing several repetitions.
regressions: Allow players to stop and reset after every kick.
Slow the pace of the activity.
Demonstrate the technique again before restarting.
successIndicators: Maintain balance throughout the kicking action.
matchApplication:
The drop punt is the primary kicking technique used throughout Australian Football.
This drill develops the technical foundation required for:
Maintaining possession.
Passing to teammates.
Kicking inside 50.
Defensive exits.
Goal kicking.
General field kicking.
Every advanced kicking drill in the AFCRL builds upon the skills developed in KK-001.

title: Stationary Drop Punt Gates
objective: Develop kicking accuracy by teaching players to consistently execute a drop punt through a defined target gate while maintaining correct kicking technique. This drill reinforces the importance of accuracy before increasing kicking distance or introducing movement.
players:
Minimum: 2
Ideal: 10–20
Maximum: Unlimited (working in pairs)
equipment: Additional cones to separate pairs if required.
setup:
Players work in pairs facing each other.
Place two cones approximately 1 metre apart halfway between each pair to create a kicking gate.
Player spacing should be:
Under 8–10: 8–10 metres apart.
Under 12–14: 10–15 metres apart.
Under 16 and above: 15–20 metres apart.
Ensure enough space exists between pairs to avoid footballs crossing into neighbouring groups.
howTheDrillWorks:
Player A begins with the football.
Player A performs a stationary drop punt towards Player B.
The football must pass cleanly through the cone gate before reaching Player B.
Player B marks or gathers the football.
Player B resets before returning the kick through the same gate.
Continue for the allocated time.
Coaches may award one point for every kick that travels cleanly through the gate without touching a cone.
The emphasis should remain on correct kicking technique rather than scoring points.
coachingPoints: Focus on one coaching point at a time.
Maintain the same technique used in KK-001.
Keep the hips and shoulders aligned with the target.
Guide the football directly onto the kicking foot.
Strike through the centre of the football.
Finish with the kicking foot pointing towards the target.
Remind players that a smooth, technically correct kick is more important than a powerful kick.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the football travels through the gate.
Provide one coaching correction before allowing the player several opportunities to practise the adjustment.
progressions: Complete the drill using the non-preferred foot.
Reduce the preparation time before kicking.
regressions: Allow players to stop and reset before every kick.
Demonstrate the technique again before restarting.
successIndicators: Kick the football through the gate.
Demonstrate improved accuracy over successive attempts.
matchApplication: During a match, players are frequently required to pass the football through narrow spaces between opponents. This drill develops the accuracy required to identify and execute those kicks while maintaining sound drop punt technique.

title: Partner Accuracy Challenge
objective: Develop the ability to consistently deliver the football to a teammate's advantage by improving kicking accuracy, control and judgement of kicking weight. Players learn that an effective pass is one that allows the receiver to mark or gather the football with minimal movement.
players:
Minimum: 2
Ideal: 10–20
Maximum: Unlimited (working in pairs)
setup:
Players work in pairs facing each other.
Players should stand:
Under 8–10: 8–10 metres apart.
Under 12–14: 10–15 metres apart.
Under 16 and above: 15–20 metres apart.
Each pair should have sufficient space to kick safely without interfering with neighbouring groups.
The receiving player should remain stationary throughout the drill.
howTheDrillWorks:
Player A kicks to Player B.
The objective is to deliver the football directly to Player B's chest without requiring them to move their feet.
Player B marks or gathers the football.
Player B immediately returns the kick using the same objective.
Continue for the allocated time.
Coaches may introduce a simple scoring system:
2 points for a chest mark.
1 point if the receiver gathers the football cleanly after one bounce.
0 points if the receiver must move significantly or the football misses the target.
The emphasis should remain on quality rather than competition.
coachingPoints: Focus on one coaching point at a time.
Look at the target before beginning the kicking action.
Kick to where the receiver can comfortably mark the football.
Match the force of the kick to the required distance.
Maintain the same drop punt technique regardless of distance.
Stay balanced throughout the kicking action.
Players should understand that kicking accurately is more important than kicking hard.
coachingCues: "Kick to your teammate, not at them."
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the receiver is forced to move.
Encourage players to evaluate each kick before receiving coaching feedback.
regressions: Encourage players to stop and reset after each kick.
successIndicators: Deliver the football directly to the receiver.
Require minimal movement from the receiver.
Demonstrate good judgement of kicking weight.
Improve accuracy over the duration of the drill.
matchApplication: Most possessions in Australian Football involve passing to a teammate under little or no pressure. This drill develops the fundamental ability to consistently hit a teammate's preferred side, allowing the next possession to be completed quickly and efficiently.

title: Distance Progression
objective: Develop a player's ability to vary the distance of a drop punt while maintaining consistent kicking technique. Players learn to adjust the power of the kick without changing the mechanics of the skill.
players:
Minimum: 2
Ideal: 10–20
Maximum: Unlimited (working in pairs)
setup:
Players work in pairs.
Mark four kicking distances using cones.
Recommended distances:
Under 10: 10 m, 15 m, 20 m, 25 m
Under 12–14: 15 m, 20 m, 25 m, 30 m
Under 16 and above: 20 m, 30 m, 40 m, 50 m
Players begin at the shortest distance.
howTheDrillWorks:
Players complete five accurate kicks from the first distance.
Once successful, both players move back to the next marker.
Continue progressing until the maximum distance is reached.
If technique deteriorates significantly, return to the previous successful distance before attempting the longer kick again.
Players should never sacrifice technique simply to complete a longer kick.
coachingPoints: Focus on one coaching point at a time.
Use exactly the same kicking mechanics regardless of distance.
Generate additional distance by increasing leg speed rather than changing the ball drop.
Maintain balance throughout the kicking action.
Keep the head over the football.
Explain that longer kicks should feel like a stronger version of the same movement rather than a completely different kick.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether technique changes as distance increases.
Watch for players trying to "muscle" the football instead of accelerating smoothly through the kick.
progressions: Complete the drill using the non-preferred foot.
Introduce target gates at each distance.
regressions: Allow players to repeat each distance until comfortable.
Reduce the number of successful kicks required before progressing.
successIndicators: Maintain correct kicking technique at every distance.
Increase kicking distance without sacrificing balance.
Demonstrate confidence at progressively longer distances.
matchApplication:
Footballers constantly adjust the length of their kicks depending on field position and available options.
This drill develops the ability to judge kicking weight accurately, allowing players to execute short passes, medium passes and longer field kicks using the same reliable drop punt technique.

title: Non-Preferred Foot Development
objective: Develop confidence and basic competence when kicking with the non-preferred foot. Players practise the same drop punt technique used on their preferred side while working at a shorter distance and lower intensity.
setup:
Players work in pairs facing each other.
Recommended starting distances:
Under 8–10: 6–8 metres apart.
Under 12–14: 8–10 metres apart.
Under 16 and above: 10–15 metres apart.
Players begin with the football in the hands they would normally use when kicking on their non-preferred side.
Spread pairs evenly so inaccurate kicks do not interfere with nearby players.
howTheDrillWorks:
Player A performs a stationary drop punt using the non-preferred foot.
Player B marks or gathers the football.
Player B resets and returns the kick using their non-preferred foot.
Players continue at a controlled pace.
After several repetitions, players may alternate between preferred and non-preferred feet.
If technique breaks down, reduce the distance.
Players should not be expected to kick the same distance with both feet immediately.
The emphasis is on clean contact, balance and confidence.
coachingPoints: Focus on one coaching point at a time.
Hold the football correctly for the non-preferred side.
Guide the football directly over the non-preferred kicking foot.
Keep the head and chest over the football.
Accept reduced distance while technique develops.
Encourage patience. The non-preferred foot will initially feel less natural.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the football is held over the correct kicking foot.
Whether the player is trying to kick too far.
Provide positive reinforcement for technically sound attempts, even when the kick misses the target.
progressions: Add a cone gate between players.
Alternate preferred and non-preferred feet every kick.
Introduce a short approach before kicking.
regressions: Allow players to practise the ball drop without kicking.
Use a stationary target rather than a partner.
successIndicators: Guide the football onto the non-preferred foot.
Deliver the football close to the intended target.
Show increased willingness to use the non-preferred side.
matchApplication:
Players are often forced onto their non-preferred side by opponents, boundary lines or body position.
This drill develops the confidence required to avoid stopping, turning unnecessarily or using a predictable kicking option during a match.

title: Kick and Follow
objective: Teach players to move immediately after disposing of the football rather than remaining stationary. Players kick to a teammate, follow their kick and rotate continuously through the drill.
groundSize:
Small to Medium Area
Approximately 25 m × 15 m per group
setup:
Create two lines facing each other.
Place one cone at the front of each line.
Recommended distance between lines:
Under 8–10: 10 metres.
Under 12–14: 15 metres.
Under 16 and above: 20 metres.
Place a second cone approximately three metres behind each front cone to organise the waiting players.
The football begins with the first player in one line.
howTheDrillWorks:
Player A kicks to Player B at the opposite line.
Player A immediately follows the kick by running to the back of Player B’s line.
Player B marks or gathers the football.
Player B resets and kicks to the next player in the opposite line.
Player B follows the kick to the back of that line.
The drill continues in a continuous pattern.
Players should communicate the intended target before kicking.
coachingPoints: Prepare the football before reaching the kicking point.
Kick accurately to the receiver’s advantage.
Run past the receiver rather than stopping in the middle.
Maintain appropriate spacing in the lines.
The drill should flow continuously without players standing in the kicking lane.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether players move immediately after disposal.
Players crossing through the kicking lane.
If lines become long, create additional groups.
progressions: Require players to use the non-preferred foot.
Add a short lead before receiving.
Add a handball before the kick.
regressions: Allow players to walk after kicking.
Remove the follow run until kicking accuracy improves.
Use a stationary partner drill first.
matchApplication:
Players must continue working after disposal during a match.
Following the football can create:
A handball receive.
An overlap.
Support at the next contest.
Defensive cover if possession is lost.

title: Triangle Kicking
objective: Develop the ability to kick accurately at changing angles rather than directly forward. Players learn to adjust their body position, identify the next target and move the football around a triangular pattern.
groundSize:
Small to Medium Area
Approximately 20 m × 20 m × 20 m
setup:
Place three cones in a triangle.
Recommended side lengths:
Under 8–10: 10–12 metres.
Under 12–14: 15 metres.
Under 16 and above: 20 metres.
Divide players evenly between the three cones.
The football begins at one cone.
All kicks initially travel in the same direction around the triangle.
howTheDrillWorks:
Player A kicks to Player B at the next cone.
Player A follows the kick to the back of Player B’s line.
Player B marks or gathers the football.
Player B turns, identifies Player C and kicks to the next cone.
Player B follows the kick.
The pattern continues around the triangle.
Change direction after several minutes.
Players should turn their body before beginning the kicking action.
coachingPoints: Look towards the next target before receiving.
Mark the football in front of the eyes.
Turn the hips and shoulders towards the target.
Encourage players to avoid catching, stopping completely and then searching for the next target.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether players drift inside the triangle.
progressions: Reverse direction on the coach’s call.
Require non-preferred foot kicking on one side.
regressions: Allow players to handball around the triangle first.
Place a coach at each cone to guide the rotation.
successIndicators: Turn towards the correct kicking direction.
Deliver accurate kicks at different angles.
matchApplication:
Australian Football rarely requires players to kick in a perfectly straight line.
This drill develops the ability to move the football around opponents, change angles and connect with teammates positioned across the ground.

title: Continuous Kicking Circuit
objective: Combine accurate kicking, marking and movement in a continuous drill. Players learn to prepare quickly, dispose of the football and move immediately to the next position.
setup:
Place four cones in a square or diamond.
Recommended spacing:
Under 10: 12–15 metres.
Under 12–14: 15–20 metres.
Under 16 and above: 20–25 metres.
Divide players evenly between the four cones.
Place one football at two opposite cones.
All footballs initially travel in the same direction.
howTheDrillWorks:
The first players at the two starting cones kick simultaneously to the next cone.
Each kicker follows the football to the back of the receiving line.
The receivers mark or gather the football.
They turn, identify the next target and kick to the following cone.
The footballs continue around the circuit.
Players follow every kick.
Change direction after several minutes.
Players must remain aware of both footballs and avoid entering another player’s kicking lane.
coachingPoints: Accuracy should be maintained before speed is increased.
progressions: Reverse direction on the coach’s call.
Require non-preferred foot kicking on selected sides.
Add a moving lead at each cone.
Add a handball receive before each kick.
regressions: Walk through the circuit before increasing pace.
Pause after each kick until players understand the rotation.
successIndicators: Keep the circuit moving without unnecessary stoppages.
matchApplication:
Australian Football requires players to make repeated decisions and execute skills without standing still.
This drill develops the ability to:
Move after disposal.
Connect multiple possessions.
Scan before receiving.
Maintain skill execution during continuous movement.

title: Moving Target Kicking
objective: Teach players to kick accurately to a teammate who is moving rather than standing still. Players learn to place the football into the receiver’s running path so they can mark without slowing down or changing direction.
setup:
Create two lines facing each other approximately 20 metres apart.
Place a starting cone five metres to the side of each receiving line.
The first receiver starts at the side cone rather than directly in front of the kicker.
The football begins with the first player in the opposite line.
howTheDrillWorks:
The receiver begins at the side cone.
The receiver leads diagonally into the space between the two lines.
The kicker waits until the receiver begins moving.
The kicker delivers the football in front of the receiver.
The receiver marks while continuing forward.
The receiver carries the football to the opposite line.
The kicker moves to the receiving line.
The drill repeats in the opposite direction.
The lead should begin before the kick is released.
coachingPoints: Kick to where the receiver is going.
Place the football slightly in front of the receiver.
Match the weight of the kick to the speed of the lead.
Avoid kicking directly at the receiver’s current position.
The receiver should accelerate into the football rather than waiting underneath it.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Timing between the lead and kick.
progressions: Increase the speed of the lead.
Add a passive defender following the receiver.
regressions: Allow the receiver to walk through the pattern.
Stop and reset after each repetition.
successIndicators: Allow the receiver to maintain speed.
Time the kick with the lead.
Deliver the football at a markable height.
matchApplication:
Players regularly kick to teammates who are leading into space.
Accurate placement allows the receiver to:
Mark without slowing down.
Play on quickly.
Maintain attacking momentum.
Avoid nearby defenders.

title: Lead and Pass
objective: Develop the connection between the kicker and a leading teammate. Players learn when to begin a lead, where to lead and how to deliver the football to the receiver’s advantage.
setup:
Create three positions:
Kicker.
Leading player.
Return player.
Place the kicker and return player approximately 25 metres apart.
Place the leading player at a starting cone 10–15 metres to the side of the target area.
Players form lines at each position.
howTheDrillWorks:
The leading player waits until the kicker has the football and is ready.
The leading player accelerates towards the open space.
The leading player calls for the football.
The kicker delivers the pass in front of the lead.
The leading player marks the football.
The leading player turns and kicks to the return player.
Players rotate:
Kicker becomes leader.
Leader becomes return player.
Return player becomes kicker.
Repeat from the opposite side after several minutes.
coachingPoints: Delay the lead until the kicker is ready.
Kick to the space in front of the leader.
Avoid kicking over the receiver’s head.
Turn and prepare quickly after marking.
The kicker and leader must work together.
A good lead can still fail if the kick is late, and a good kick can fail if the lead is poorly timed.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the leader is forced to stop.
progressions: Allow the leader to choose between two directions.
Require a quick play-on after the mark.
Use the non-preferred foot when the lead goes to one side.
regressions: Allow the leader to walk through the pattern.
successIndicators: Deliver the football in front of the receiver.
matchApplication:
This drill replicates the basic connection between a ball carrier and a teammate leading into space.
It applies to:
Forward leads.
Wing outlets.
Defensive exits.
Centre corridor movement.
Short possession kicks.

title: Kicking to Multiple Leads
objective: Develop the kicker’s ability to identify and select between multiple leading targets. Players learn to scan before receiving, recognise the best available option and deliver the football to the selected receiver’s advantage.
setup:
Create one kicking position and two leading lanes.
Place the kicker approximately 25 metres from the target area.
Set two starting cones approximately 10 metres apart for the leading players.
Place a waiting line behind each leading cone.
A feeder stands five to ten metres behind the kicker with the football.
howTheDrillWorks:
The feeder passes the football to the kicker.
As the kicker receives the football, the first player from each leading line begins a lead.
One player leads left and the other leads right.
The kicker scans both options and selects one target.
The kicker delivers the football to the selected player’s advantage.
The selected receiver marks the football and returns it to the feeder.
The unselected player completes the lead before returning to the back of their line.
The kicker rotates into one of the leading lines.
A new kicker moves into position.
Continue for the allocated time.
The coach should vary which lead appears to be the better option.
coachingPoints: Focus on one coaching point at a time.
Keep both leading options within vision.
Select the player with the greatest space.
Kick to where the receiver is moving.
Avoid staring at the selected target too early.
Deliver the football at a markable height.
The drill should reward correct decisions as well as accurate execution.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the kicker scans before receiving.
Whether the kicker consistently favours one side.
Whether unselected players complete their leads.
Provide feedback on the decision before focusing on the execution.
progressions: Add a passive defender between the leading players.
Allow leading players to choose their own direction.
Require non-preferred foot use when selecting one side.
regressions: Use one leading option at a time.
Tell the kicker which option to select.
Allow the kicker to begin with the football.
successIndicators: Select the player in the greatest space.
Make decisions before the lead is completed.
Deliver the football to the receiver’s advantage.
matchApplication:
Ball carriers regularly have several teammates presenting at the same time.
This drill develops the ability to identify the best option rather than automatically kicking to the first player seen or the loudest voice.

title: Lead Direction Decision
objective: Teach players to recognise and respond to a receiver who can lead in more than one direction. The kicker must delay the decision until the receiver commits to a lead and then place the football into the correct space.
setup:
Place one kicking cone approximately 25 metres from the leading area.
Place one starting cone for the receiver directly ahead of the kicker.
Place two target cones approximately eight metres apart, one to the left and one to the right of the receiver’s starting position.
Players form one line at the kicking cone and one line at the receiver’s starting cone.
howTheDrillWorks:
The first kicker begins with the football.
The receiver starts facing the kicker.
On the coach’s call, the receiver chooses to lead towards either the left or right target cone.
The kicker reads the direction of the lead.
The kicker delivers the football into the receiver’s path.
The receiver marks or gathers the football.
The receiver returns the football to the kicking line.
The kicker moves to the receiver’s line.
The receiver returns to the back of the kicking line.
Continue for the allocated time.
The coach should ensure lead directions vary rather than follow a predictable pattern.
coachingPoints: Focus on one coaching point at a time.
Avoid deciding before the receiver moves.
Read the receiver’s first committed steps.
Turn the hips and shoulders towards the selected target.
Kick into the space ahead of the receiver.
The kicker should remain balanced while waiting for the lead to develop.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the kicker guesses the direction.
Reaction time after the lead begins.
Whether players remain balanced while waiting.
Encourage the kicker to react calmly rather than rush.
progressions: Increase the speed of the lead.
Allow the receiver to lead forward, left or right.
Require the kicker to receive a handball before making the decision.
regressions: Tell the kicker the lead direction before the repetition.
Reduce the distance between kicker and receiver.
Slow the receiver to walking pace.
Use only one direction for several repetitions.
Allow the kicker additional preparation time.
successIndicators: Wait until the lead direction is clear.
Align the body with the selected target.
Deliver the football at a markable height.
matchApplication:
Receivers frequently change their leading direction based on space, defenders and ball-carrier position.
This drill develops the patience and awareness required to read the lead rather than forcing the receiver towards a predetermined location.

title: Kick to Space
objective: Develop the ability to kick the football into open space rather than directly at a teammate. Players learn to recognise where the receiver can move next and place the football in a location that maintains attacking momentum.
equipment: Optional flat markers for target zones.
setup:
Create one kicking cone and three target zones.
Place the target zones approximately 20–30 metres from the kicker:
One directly ahead.
One to the left.
One to the right.
Each target zone should be approximately four metres wide and six metres long.
A receiver begins approximately five metres behind the target zones.
Players form lines at the kicking and receiving positions.
howTheDrillWorks:
The kicker begins with the football.
The receiver moves forward and selects one of the three target zones.
The kicker identifies the receiver’s movement.
The kicker places the football into the selected target zone.
The receiver marks or gathers the football while continuing through the zone.
The receiver returns the football to the kicking line.
Players rotate positions.
Continue for the allocated time.
The receiver should not stop inside the zone and wait for the football.
coachingPoints: Focus on one coaching point at a time.
Place the football ahead of the receiver.
Keep the kick away from imaginary defensive pressure.
Select a flatter kick when the receiver is moving quickly.
Avoid forcing the receiver to stop or move backwards.
Explain that the target is the space, not the player’s current body position.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the kicker watches the receiver.
Whether players kick directly at the receiver.
Praise well-placed kicks even when the receiver does not mark cleanly.
progressions: Reduce the size of the target zones.
Allow the receiver to change direction.
Require non-preferred foot kicking to selected zones.
regressions: Tell the receiver which zone to use.
Slow the receiver to jogging pace.
Allow the kicker to begin closer to the target.
successIndicators: Place the football ahead of the receiver.
Allow the receiver to maintain speed.
Avoid kicking directly at the player.
matchApplication:
Effective teams often kick to space rather than to stationary teammates.
This skill is used during:
Forward entries.
Wing transitions.
Defensive exits.
Fast breaks.
Kicks over or around defensive pressure.

title: Running Drop Punt
objective: Develop the ability to execute an accurate drop punt while running at controlled speed. Players learn to prepare the football early, manage their final steps and maintain forward momentum through the kick.
groundSize:
Medium Area
Approximately 35 m × 20 m per lane
setup:
Create a straight kicking lane.
Place:
A starting cone.
A kicking cone 10 metres ahead.
A receiving cone 15–25 metres beyond the kicking cone.
Players form lines at the starting and receiving cones.
The football begins with the first player at the starting cone.
howTheDrillWorks:
Player A runs from the starting cone while carrying the football.
Player A prepares the football before reaching the kicking cone.
Player A executes a drop punt while continuing forward.
Player B marks or gathers the football at the receiving cone.
Player A continues running to the back of the receiving line.
Player B carries the football to the opposite starting position or returns the kick through a second lane.
Continue for the allocated time.
Players should begin at controlled pace before progressing towards game speed.
coachingPoints: Focus on one coaching point at a time.
Prepare the ball before the final steps.
Maintain the head over the football.
Accuracy should be established before maximum running speed is introduced.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether players slow excessively or rush.
Adjust the distance between cones to suit the age and ability of the group.
successIndicators: Execute without significantly slowing before the kick.
matchApplication:
Running drop punts are used throughout general play when players:
Break from congestion.
Carry the football through space.
Deliver inside 50.
Exit defence.
Complete an overlap.
Attack through the corridor.

title: Short Approach Drop Punt
primarySkill: Drop Punt from a Short Approach
objective: Progress players from stationary kicking to executing a drop punt after a short, controlled approach. Players learn to coordinate their steps, ball preparation and kicking action without rushing.
groundSize:
Small to Medium Area
Approximately 25 m × 20 m
setup:
Players work in pairs facing each other.
Place a starting cone approximately three metres behind each player’s kicking cone.
Recommended kicking distances:
Under 8–10: 8–10 metres.
Under 12–14: 12–15 metres.
Under 16 and above: 15–20 metres.
Players begin at the rear starting cone.
howTheDrillWorks:
Player A begins with the football at the starting cone.
Player A walks or jogs forward for two to four controlled steps.
Player A performs a drop punt from the kicking cone.
Player B marks or gathers the football.
Player B resets at their starting cone.
Player B repeats the short approach and kick.
Continue for the allocated time.
Increase approach speed only when technique remains consistent.
The approach should remain controlled rather than becoming a sprint.
coachingPoints: Focus on one coaching point at a time.
Prepare the football during the approach.
Guide the football onto the boot.
Avoid taking an excessively long final step.
Continue moving naturally after the kick.
The kicking action should remain similar to the stationary drop punt.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the player rushes as speed increases.
Reduce the approach speed if technique deteriorates.
progressions: Progress to a continuous running kick.
Receive a handball before beginning the approach.
regressions: Allow players to rehearse the steps without the football.
successIndicators: Coordinate the approach and kicking action.
matchApplication:
Players rarely kick from a completely stationary position during general play.
This drill introduces the movement coordination required to prepare and execute the football while approaching the point of disposal.

title: Receive, Run and Kick
objective: Develop the ability to receive the football, move quickly into space and execute an accurate kick. Players learn to prepare the next action before taking possession and avoid unnecessary delays after the mark or gather.
setup:
Create three stations in a straight or slightly angled line:
Feeder.
Receiver.
Final target.
Place the feeder and receiver approximately 15 metres apart.
Place the final target approximately 20 metres beyond the receiver.
Players form lines at all three stations.
The football begins with the feeder.
howTheDrillWorks:
The feeder kicks to the receiver.
Before the football arrives, the receiver scans towards the final target.
The receiver marks or gathers the football.
The receiver immediately runs forward for five to ten metres.
The receiver delivers a running drop punt to the final target.
The final target marks the football.
Players rotate:
Feeder becomes receiver.
Receiver becomes final target.
Final target returns to the feeder line.
Continue for the allocated time.
The receiver should prepare the next decision before taking possession.
coachingPoints: Focus on one coaching point at a time.
Mark the football in front of the eyes.
Deliver the football to the final target’s advantage.
Encourage quick but controlled movement rather than rushed disposal.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the receiver scans before possession.
Speed of movement after the mark.
The coach should distinguish between fast decision making and hurried execution.
progressions: Require a bounce during the run.
regressions: Allow the receiver to walk after marking.
Remove the initial kick and begin with a handball.
Pause after the mark before beginning the run.
matchApplication:
Players often receive possession and must immediately carry the football before delivering to the next teammate.
This drill applies to:
Half-back rebound.
Wing transition.
Centre-square exits.
Overlap running.
Forward entries.
Switching play.

title: Running Kick Through Gates
objective: Develop accurate kicking while running by requiring players to execute a drop punt through a target gate. Players learn to control their final steps, align their body and maintain accuracy without stopping before disposal.
players: Minimum: 4 Ideal: 8–16 Maximum: 20 using multiple lanes
groundSize:
Medium Area
Approximately 35 m × 15 m per lane
setup:
Create a straight running lane.
Place:
A starting cone.
A kicking cone approximately 10 metres ahead.
A two-metre-wide target gate approximately 10 metres beyond the kicking cone.
A receiving cone five to ten metres beyond the gate.
Players form lines at the starting and receiving cones.
The football begins at the starting line.
howTheDrillWorks:
Player A runs from the starting cone with the football.
Player A prepares the football before reaching the kicking cone.
Player A performs a running drop punt through the target gate.
Player B marks or gathers the football beyond the gate.
Player A continues to the back of Player B’s line.
Player B returns through the opposite lane or carries the football to the starting line.
Continue for the allocated time.
Reverse the lane direction so players practise kicking from both sides.
Players score one point each time the football travels cleanly through the gate.
coachingPoints: Focus on one coaching point at a time.
Prepare the football before the final steps.
Keep the hips and shoulders aligned with the gate.
Guide the football directly onto the kicking foot.
Finish with the kicking leg pointing towards the target.
Accuracy should remain the priority as running speed increases.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the football passes through the gate.
Whether players slow excessively before kicking.
Reduce speed or widen the gate if technique begins to deteriorate.
progressions: Introduce a moving receiver beyond the gate.
regressions: Allow players to jog rather than run.
matchApplication:
Players often carry the football through space before kicking between opponents or into a narrow passing lane.
This drill develops the accuracy required to complete those kicks without losing attacking speed.

title: Bounce and Kick
objective: Develop the ability to complete a controlled running bounce before preparing and executing an accurate drop punt. Players learn to regain possession cleanly and transition smoothly from running to kicking.
players: Minimum: 4 Ideal: 8–16 Maximum: 20 using multiple lanes
groundSize:
Medium Area
Approximately 40 m × 15 m per lane
setup:
Create a straight lane.
Place:
A starting cone.
A bounce cone approximately 10 metres ahead.
A kicking cone another eight to ten metres ahead.
A receiving cone 15–25 metres beyond the kicking cone.
Players form lines at the starting and receiving cones.
howTheDrillWorks:
Player A runs from the starting cone carrying the football.
Player A completes one running bounce near the bounce cone.
Player A regathers the football cleanly.
Player A prepares the football before reaching the kicking cone.
Player A performs a running drop punt to Player B.
Player B marks or gathers the football.
Player A continues to the receiving line.
Player B returns through the opposite lane or carries the football back to the start.
Continue for the allocated time.
The bounce should be completed early enough to allow time for controlled ball preparation.
coachingPoints: Focus on one coaching point at a time.
Bounce the football in front of the body.
Keep the bounce low and controlled.
Secure possession before preparing to kick.
Avoid rushing immediately after the bounce.
Players should not bounce too close to the kicking point.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether players look down for too long.
Move the bounce cone if players do not have enough time to prepare.
progressions: Require the player to choose between kicking targets.
regressions: Reduce the distance of the run.
Allow players to bounce and stop before kicking.
matchApplication:
Players frequently need to bounce while carrying the football before disposing.
This drill develops the coordination required to maintain speed, meet the running-bounce requirement and execute the next kick accurately.

title: Handball Receive and Kick
objective: Develop the ability to receive a handball while moving and quickly transition into an accurate kick. Players learn to time their support run, receive cleanly and prepare the football without breaking stride.
players: Minimum: 6 Ideal: 9–18 Maximum: 24 using multiple groups
setup:
Create three positions:
Ball carrier.
Support runner.
Kicking target.
Place the support runner’s starting cone approximately five metres beside and behind the ball carrier.
Place the kicking target 20–30 metres ahead.
Players form lines at all three positions.
The football begins with the ball carrier.
howTheDrillWorks:
The ball carrier begins jogging forward.
The support runner accelerates alongside and calls for the football.
The ball carrier handballs into the support runner’s path.
The support runner receives without stopping.
The support runner carries the football for several steps.
The support runner kicks to the final target.
Players rotate:
Ball carrier becomes support runner.
Support runner becomes final target.
Final target returns to the ball-carrier line.
Repeat from the opposite side after several minutes.
The handball should allow the receiver to maintain forward momentum.
coachingPoints: Focus on one coaching point at a time.
Receive the football in front of the body.
Move the football into kicking position early.
Kick to the final target’s advantage.
The receiver should not be forced to reach behind or slow down.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Coach the quality of the handball as well as the kick.
progressions: Require the receiver to use the non-preferred foot.
Begin with a ground ball gather.
Add a second handball before the kick.
regressions: Allow players to stop after receiving.
Remove the final target and kick through a wide gate.
matchApplication:
This drill replicates an overlap or release handball where the receiving player becomes the next kicker.
It applies to:
Half-back rebound.
Midfield overlap.
Corridor attack.
Forward entries.
Exiting congestion.

title: Turn and Kick
objective: Develop the ability to receive the football facing away from the intended target, turn efficiently and execute an accurate kick. Players learn to scan before possession and reposition the body without losing balance.
players: Minimum: 6 Ideal: 9–18 Maximum: 24 using multiple groups
setup:
Create three positions in a straight line:
Feeder.
Receiver.
Final target.
The receiver begins with their back or side facing the final target.
Place the feeder approximately 10–15 metres from the receiver.
Place the final target approximately 20 metres beyond the receiver.
Players form lines at each position.
howTheDrillWorks:
The receiver scans over the shoulder towards the final target.
The feeder kicks or handballs to the receiver.
The receiver marks or gathers the football.
The receiver turns towards the final target.
The receiver balances and delivers an accurate kick.
The final target marks the football.
Players rotate through each position.
Change the turning direction after several repetitions.
Players should scan before the football arrives rather than waiting until after possession.
coachingPoints: Focus on one coaching point at a time.
Align the hips and shoulders with the target.
Players should use the most efficient turn for the situation.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Require players to practise turning both ways.
progressions: Allow the final target to move.
Require a turn onto the non-preferred side.
Receive a ground ball instead of a pass.
Reduce the time allowed to dispose.
regressions: Tell players which direction to turn.
Allow the receiver to stop after turning.
successIndicators: Deliver accurate kicks in both directions.
matchApplication:
Players frequently receive the football while facing away from goal or the next target.
This skill applies to:
Marks on the boundary.
Ground balls in congestion.
Defensive switches.
Midfield possessions.
Forward entries after turning from pressure.

title: Overlap Run and Kick
objective: Develop the ability to create an overlap, receive a handball at speed and deliver an accurate kick. Players learn to time their supporting run so they receive the football in front of the original ball carrier and continue the attacking movement.
players: Minimum: 6 Ideal: 9–18 Maximum: 24 using multiple groups
setup:
Create three positions:
Initial ball carrier.
Overlap runner.
Final kicking target.
Place the overlap runner approximately five metres behind and to the side of the initial ball carrier.
Place the final target 25–35 metres ahead.
Players form lines at all three positions.
The football begins with the initial ball carrier.
howTheDrillWorks:
The initial ball carrier begins moving forward.
The overlap runner delays briefly before accelerating past on the outside.
The overlap runner calls for the football.
The initial ball carrier handballs into the runner’s path.
The overlap runner receives without slowing.
The overlap runner carries the football for several steps.
The overlap runner kicks to the final target.
Players rotate:
Initial ball carrier becomes overlap runner.
Overlap runner becomes final target.
Final target returns to the initial ball-carrier line.
Repeat from both sides.
The overlap runner should receive in front of the ball carrier rather than beside or behind them.
coachingPoints: Focus on one coaching point at a time.
Delay the support run until the ball carrier begins moving.
Accelerate past at the correct angle.
Receive the handball in front of the body.
Prepare the football while maintaining speed.
Deliver the kick to the target’s advantage.
The support run should create forward momentum rather than simply adding another player near the football.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: If the overlap becomes crowded, increase the distance between starting positions.
progressions: Require non-preferred foot kicking from one side.
Allow the ball carrier to decide whether to handball or retain possession.
regressions: Allow the receiver to stop before kicking.
Walk through the running pattern before increasing speed.
successIndicators: Receive in front of the ball carrier.
matchApplication:
Overlap running is used to:
Break defensive lines.
Create an extra player in attack.
Move the football from half-back.
Generate forward momentum.
Deliver inside 50 with reduced pressure.

title: Change of Direction Kick
objective: Develop the ability to change running direction before executing an accurate kick. Players learn to regain balance after cutting, prepare the football early and align their body with a new target.
players: Minimum: 4 Ideal: 8–16 Maximum: 20 using multiple lanes
setup:
Create a zigzag running lane.
Place:
A starting cone.
A direction-change cone five to eight metres ahead and to one side.
A second direction-change cone five to eight metres ahead on the opposite side.
A kicking cone beyond the second turn.
A receiving cone 15–25 metres ahead.
Players form lines at the starting and receiving positions.
howTheDrillWorks:
Player A runs from the starting cone with the football.
Player A changes direction around the first cone.
Player A changes direction again around the second cone.
Player A prepares the football before reaching the kicking cone.
Player A performs a running drop punt to Player B.
Player B marks or gathers the football.
Player A continues to the receiving line.
Player B returns through an opposite lane or carries the football back.
Change the cone pattern after several minutes.
Players should maintain control through each direction change.
coachingPoints: Focus on one coaching point at a time.
Lower the body before changing direction.
Use short steps through the turn.
Align the body with the final target.
Prepare the football before the kicking cone.
Avoid rushing after the final turn.
The kick should remain controlled even after rapid movement.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether players drift outside the lane.
Increase agility demands only when the kick remains accurate.
progressions: Add a bounce before the first turn.
Allow the coach to call the direction of the first turn.
regressions: Allow players to stop before kicking.
successIndicators: Complete the movement without unnecessary stopping.
matchApplication:
Players often need to evade pressure, change direction and then dispose of the football.
This skill is used when:
Escaping congestion.
Moving around an opponent.
Changing the angle of attack.
Creating space before a forward entry.
Rebounding from defence.

title: Ground Ball Gather and Kick
primarySkill: Kicking After a Ground Ball Gather
objective: Develop the ability to collect a ground ball cleanly, accelerate away from the contest and execute an accurate kick. Players learn to secure possession before transitioning quickly into the kicking action.
players: Minimum: 4 Ideal: 8–16 Maximum: 20 using multiple lanes
setup:
Create a straight lane.
Place:
A starting cone.
A ground-ball cone five to eight metres ahead.
A kicking cone another five to eight metres ahead.
A receiving cone 15–25 metres beyond the kicking cone.
A feeder stands beside the ground-ball cone.
Players form lines at the starting and receiving cones.
howTheDrillWorks:
Player A runs from the starting cone.
The feeder rolls the football into Player A’s path.
Player A lowers the body and gathers the football cleanly.
Player A accelerates away from the collection point.
Player A prepares the football before reaching the kicking cone.
Player A executes a running drop punt to Player B.
Player B marks or gathers the football.
Player A continues to the receiving line.
Player B returns to the starting line with the football.
Rotate the feeder regularly.
The ground ball should be rolled at a realistic but controllable speed.
coachingPoints: Focus on one coaching point at a time.
Approach the football with controlled speed.
Lower the hips and keep the head over the ball.
Gather the football cleanly before accelerating.
Take the first steps away from the collection point.
Players should not attempt to kick before possession is secure.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: If players repeatedly fumble, reduce the speed of the rolled football.
progressions: Increase the speed or angle of the ground ball.
Require the player to change direction after gathering.
Begin with a contested ground ball.
regressions: Allow the player to stop after gathering.
Remove the kicking component until collection improves.
successIndicators: Complete the sequence without unnecessary delay.
matchApplication:
Ground balls regularly begin attacking possessions.
Players must collect cleanly, escape immediate pressure and deliver accurately to a teammate.
This drill applies to:
Loose-ball wins.
Crumbing.
Contested-ball exits.
Defensive rebounds.
Midfield stoppage releases.

title: Evasion and Kick
objective: Develop the ability to evade an opponent or obstacle before executing an accurate kick. Players learn to change direction under control, protect the football and regain balance before disposal.
players: Minimum: 5 Ideal: 8–16 Maximum: 20 using multiple lanes
equipment: Optional agility pole or passive defender.
setup:
Create one running lane.
Place:
A starting cone.
An evasion point approximately eight metres ahead.
Two exit gates, one left and one right of the evasion point.
A kicking cone beyond each exit gate.
A receiving target 20–30 metres ahead.
A coach or passive defender stands at the evasion point.
Players form lines at the starting and receiving positions.
howTheDrillWorks:
Player A runs towards the evasion point with the football.
The coach or passive defender moves slightly towards one side.
Player A changes direction through the opposite exit gate.
Player A secures the football and regains balance.
Player A executes a running drop punt to Player B.
Player B marks or gathers the football.
Player A continues to the receiving line.
Player B returns to the starting line.
Change the defender’s movement regularly.
The defender provides visual pressure without tackling.
coachingPoints: Focus on one coaching point at a time.
Keep the football secure during the evasive movement.
Align with the target after the evasion.
The evasion should create space for the kick rather than force a rushed disposal.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Reduce the defender’s movement if players lose control.
progressions: Reduce the width of the exit gates.
Require the non-preferred foot after one exit.
Allow the player to use a sidestep, baulk or change of pace.
regressions: Replace the defender with a stationary pole.
Tell the player which gate to use.
Allow the player to stop before kicking.
matchApplication:
Players often need to create kicking space by:
Sidestepping an opponent.
Changing direction.
Moving around a mark.
Escaping congestion.
Avoiding frontal pressure.

title: Contested Gather and Kick
objective: Develop the ability to win or secure a contested ground ball, escape pressure and execute an effective kick. Players learn to place the body between the opponent and the football before creating enough space to dispose accurately.
players: Minimum: 6 Ideal: 10–18 Maximum: 24 using multiple groups
setup:
Create:
A feeder position.
A contest area approximately six metres wide.
Two exit gates beyond the contest.
One kicking target 20–30 metres ahead.
Two players begin on opposite sides of the contest area.
The feeder stands five to ten metres away with the football.
howTheDrillWorks:
The feeder rolls or bounces the football into the contest area.
Both players compete to gain possession.
The player who wins the football protects it and exits through either gate.
The opposing player applies controlled pressure without completing a full tackle.
The ball winner accelerates into space.
The ball winner kicks to the target.
Players reset and rotate.
Alternate opponents regularly.
The drill ends if the football becomes trapped for an extended period. Restart with a new feed.
coachingPoints: Focus on one coaching point at a time.
Approach the football with the body low.
Position the body between the opponent and the football.
Gather with two hands when possible.
The first objective is to secure possession. The second is to create space for the kick.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Stop the drill if contact becomes uncontrolled.
progressions: Require a handball receive before kicking.
Reduce the size of the exit gates.
Allow full tackling for appropriately prepared groups.
regressions: Roll the football directly towards one player.
Allow the ball winner to stop after exiting.
successIndicators: Recover quickly after losing the contest.
matchApplication:
This drill replicates possessions that begin with:
A loose ball.
A stoppage spill.
A marking contest.
A defensive ground ball.
A forward-half turnover.
Players must secure possession before creating a usable disposal.

title: Two-on-One Release Kick
objective: Develop the ability to use a two-on-one advantage to release one player into space for an effective kick. Players learn to draw the defender, support at the correct angle and identify when the kicker has been freed.
players: Minimum: 7 Ideal: 10–18 Maximum: 24 using multiple groups
setup:
Create a channel approximately 15 metres wide and 25 metres long.
Place:
Two attacking starting cones at one end.
One defender in the middle of the channel.
One final kicking target 20 metres beyond the channel.
The two attackers begin side by side, with one holding the football.
howTheDrillWorks:
The two attackers move into the channel.
The defender applies pressure and attempts to stop forward movement.
The ball carrier decides whether to:
Carry the football and draw the defender.
Handball to the support runner.
The attackers use the two-on-one advantage to release one player beyond the defender.
The released player kicks to the final target.
Players rotate through attacking, defending and target roles.
Continue for the allocated time.
The defender uses passive or controlled pressure according to the age and experience of the group.
coachingPoints: Focus on one coaching point at a time.
Draw the defender before releasing the football.
Support at an angle that allows continued movement.
Prepare quickly for the final kick.
The objective is to release the kicker, not simply complete a handball.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the released player remains free.
Pause the drill briefly if attackers repeatedly run into the same space.
progressions: Require the final kick to a moving target.
regressions: Tell attackers which player should receive.
successIndicators: Deliver accurately to the final target.
matchApplication:
Two-on-one situations occur during:
Defensive rebound.
Midfield overlap.
Forward-half transition.
Loose-ball wins.
Attacking handball chains.
Players must use the outnumber to create a less pressured kick.

title: Chaser Pressure Kick
objective: Develop the ability to execute an accurate kick while an opponent applies pressure from behind. Players learn to maintain composure, prepare the football early and use available space before the defender closes.
players: Minimum: 6 Ideal: 10–18 Maximum: 24 using multiple lanes
groundSize:
Medium Area
Approximately 40 m × 15 m per lane
setup:
Create a straight channel.
Place:
An attacker’s starting cone.
A defender’s starting cone three to five metres behind.
A kicking line 12–15 metres ahead.
A receiving target 20–30 metres beyond the kicking line.
The attacker begins with the football.
The defender starts behind and slightly to one side.
howTheDrillWorks:
On the coach’s signal, the attacker and defender begin.
The attacker accelerates towards the kicking line.
The defender chases and applies pressure without tackling.
The attacker prepares the football before the kicking line.
The attacker kicks to the target before the defender closes.
The defender continues through without contacting the kicker.
Players rotate roles.
Adjust the defender’s starting distance to create appropriate pressure.
The attacker must stay within the channel.
coachingPoints: Focus on one coaching point at a time.
Prepare the football before pressure arrives.
Complete the kick rather than simply disposing quickly.
The defender should pressure the decision without creating unsafe contact.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Adjust the starting gap so the attacker is challenged but still capable of success.
progressions: Allow controlled tackling before the kicking line.
Add a second defender approaching from the side.
regressions: Use a coach as the chaser.
matchApplication:
Chasing pressure commonly occurs when players:
Break from congestion.
Rebound from defence.
Run through the corridor.
Receive an overlap handball.
Attack an open forward line.

title: Defender Decision Kick
objective: Develop the ability to recognise how a defender is positioned and select the safest available kicking option. Players learn to scan multiple targets, identify where the defender cannot apply effective pressure and execute the kick without unnecessary delay.
players: Minimum: 8 Ideal: 12–20 Maximum: 24 using multiple groups
setup:
Create one central kicking position.
Place three receiving targets approximately 20–30 metres away:
One to the left.
One directly ahead.
One to the right.
Position one defender five to eight metres in front of the kicker.
A feeder stands behind or beside the kicker with the football.
Players form lines at the feeder, kicking and receiving positions.
howTheDrillWorks:
The feeder passes the football to the kicker.
As the kicker receives, the defender moves to block or pressure one of the three target options.
The kicker scans all available targets.
The kicker selects an option away from the defender’s pressure.
The kicker delivers the football to the chosen receiver.
The receiver marks or gathers the football.
Players rotate through the feeder, kicker, receiver and defender roles.
Continue for the allocated time.
The defender should vary which target they block.
coachingPoints: Focus on one coaching point at a time.
Avoid kicking towards the option under greatest pressure.
Move slightly if required to improve the kicking lane.
Deliver the football to the receiver’s advantage.
The best option may change immediately before possession.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the kicker scans before receiving.
Whether the kicker repeatedly favours one side.
Praise the correct decision even if the execution is imperfect.
progressions: Reduce the distance between defender and kicker.
Require the non-preferred foot for one side.
Add a time limit for disposal.
regressions: Tell the defender which option to block.
Allow the kicker to begin with the football.
successIndicators: Avoid forcing the football into pressure.
matchApplication:
Ball carriers regularly need to choose between several targets while opponents block or close passing lanes.
This drill applies to:
Defensive exits.
Forward entries.
Midfield possession.
Switching play.
Kicking from congestion.

title: Closing Defender Kick
objective: Develop the ability to execute an effective kick while a defender closes from the front. Players learn to identify the available kicking lane, prepare early and dispose before the defender reaches smothering distance.
players: Minimum: 6 Ideal: 10–18 Maximum: 24 using multiple groups
setup:
Place:
One attacker’s starting cone.
One defender’s starting cone 10–15 metres directly ahead.
Two target gates positioned left and right beyond the defender.
One receiver behind each target gate.
The attacker begins with the football.
The defender begins stationary or moving slowly towards the attacker.
howTheDrillWorks:
On the coach’s signal, the attacker moves forward.
The defender closes from the front with hands raised to create smothering pressure.
The attacker identifies the clearer target gate.
The attacker adjusts slightly left or right to create a kicking lane.
The attacker delivers the football through the chosen gate.
The defender avoids contact with the kicking leg.
Players rotate through attacking, defending and receiving roles.
Continue for the allocated time.
The defender’s role is to reduce time and space without tackling.
coachingPoints: Focus on one coaching point at a time.
Move slightly off the line of pressure.
Prepare the football before the defender arrives.
Keep the kick compact and controlled.
Avoid kicking directly into the defender.
The player does not need to make a large evasive movement. A small angle change may create the required kicking lane.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Movement away from the defender’s line.
Whether the attacker panics or retreats.
progressions: Allow the defender to choose the closing line.
Require non-preferred foot use on one side.
Allow the defender to attempt a controlled smother.
regressions: Increase the distance between attacker and defender.
Tell the attacker which target to use.
Allow the attacker to stop and kick initially.
matchApplication:
Frontal pressure occurs when players:
Exit stoppages.
Receive in traffic.
Kick inside 50.
Rebound through the corridor.
Take possession near an opponent.

title: Smother Pressure Kick
objective: Develop the ability to recognise and avoid a potential smother before executing a kick. Players learn to alter the kicking angle, delay briefly or move laterally to create a safe disposal lane.
players: Minimum: 6 Ideal: 10–18 Maximum: 24 using multiple groups
setup:
Place one attacker’s cone and one defender’s cone approximately six to eight metres apart.
Place two kicking gates, one left and one right of the defender.
Position a receiver 20–25 metres beyond each gate.
The attacker begins with the football.
The defender begins facing the attacker.
howTheDrillWorks:
On the coach’s signal, the attacker moves forward.
The defender closes and raises the hands to threaten a smother.
The attacker reads the defender’s movement.
The attacker creates a safe kicking lane by:
Moving slightly left or right.
Taking an extra step.
Delaying until the defender loses balance.
The attacker kicks through one of the two gates to a receiver.
The defender attempts a controlled smother without contacting the kicking leg.
Players rotate roles.
Continue for the allocated time.
The defender should pressure the kick realistically while maintaining safety.
coachingPoints: Focus on one coaching point at a time.
Avoid kicking directly through raised hands.
Complete the kick only when the lane is clear.
The objective is not always to kick immediately.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether players expose the kicking leg.
Stop the drill if smother attempts become uncontrolled.
progressions: Allow the defender to recover after the first evasion.
regressions: Tell the attacker which side to use.
Have the defender hold a hit shield rather than attempt a smother.
matchApplication:
Smother pressure commonly occurs when players:
Exit congestion.
Kick from stoppages.
Deliver inside 50.
Receive near an opponent.
Attempt defensive clearances.

title: Time-Limited Kick
objective: Develop the ability to scan, select a target and execute an accurate kick within a limited period. Players learn to prepare before possession and avoid wasting time once the football is secured.
players: Minimum: 6 Ideal: 10–18 Maximum: 24 using multiple groups
setup:
Place one central receiving cone.
Position three targets approximately 20 metres away at different angles.
A feeder stands 10–15 metres from the central receiver.
Players form lines at the feeder, receiver and target positions.
howTheDrillWorks:
The receiver scans the target positions.
The feeder passes the football to the receiver.
As the football arrives, the coach begins a countdown.
The receiver must select and kick to a target within the allowed time.
Recommended time limits:
Under 12: Four seconds.
Under 14: Three seconds.
Under 16 and above: Two to three seconds.
The selected target marks or gathers the football.
Players rotate positions.
Continue for the allocated time.
The coach may nominate that one target is unavailable immediately before possession.
coachingPoints: Focus on one coaching point at a time.
The time limit should challenge decision speed without making accurate execution impossible.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Adjust the countdown to match player ability.
progressions: Remove one option on the coach’s call.
Require the non-preferred foot for selected targets.
Begin with a ground ball gather.
regressions: Allow the receiver to begin with the football.
matchApplication:
Players often have limited time after:
Taking possession in traffic.
Receiving at half-back.
Winning a clearance.
Marking and playing on.
Collecting a loose football.

title: Kick Under Side Pressure
objective: Develop the ability to execute an effective kick while pressure arrives from the side. Players learn to protect the football, maintain their line and avoid being pushed across the intended target.
players: Minimum: 6 Ideal: 10–18 Maximum: 24 using multiple lanes
setup:
Create a straight running lane.
Place:
An attacker’s starting cone.
A defender’s starting cone three metres to the attacker’s left or right.
A kicking line 10–12 metres ahead.
A receiving target 20–30 metres beyond the kicking line.
The attacker begins with the football.
The defender begins slightly behind and to the side.
howTheDrillWorks:
On the coach’s signal, both players begin.
The attacker runs towards the kicking line.
The defender applies controlled side pressure using body positioning or a hit shield.
The attacker protects the football and maintains forward movement.
The attacker prepares and kicks to the target.
The defender avoids contacting the kicking leg.
Players rotate roles.
Repeat with pressure arriving from both sides.
The contact level must remain appropriate to the group.
coachingPoints: Focus on one coaching point at a time.
Keep the football on the side away from pressure.
Use the body to protect possession.
Avoid leaning excessively into the defender.
Regain balance before the final step.
Align the kick with the target.
The attacker should absorb pressure without losing technical control.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the defender enters the kicking-leg area.
Reduce pressure immediately if player safety is affected.
regressions: Replace the defender with a hit shield held by a coach.
Allow the attacker to stop before kicking.
successIndicators: Perform effectively from both pressure sides.
matchApplication:
Lateral pressure occurs when players:
Run along the boundary.
Exit congestion.
Receive an overlap handball.
Break from a tackle.
Carry the football through traffic.

title: One-Step Kick
objective: Develop the ability to execute an accurate drop punt using only one controlled step. Players learn to prepare the football early and use a compact kicking action when time and space are limited.
players: Minimum: 2 Ideal: 8–20 Maximum: Unlimited, working in pairs
setup:
Players work in pairs facing each other.
Recommended distances:
Under 12–14: 10–12 metres.
Under 16 and above: 12–18 metres.
Place one kicking cone in front of each player.
The football begins with one player.
howTheDrillWorks:
Player A receives or begins with the football.
Player A prepares the ball immediately.
Player A takes one controlled step.
Player A executes a drop punt to Player B.
Player B marks or gathers the football.
Player B repeats the same one-step kick.
Continue for the allocated time.
Alternate preferred and non-preferred feet where appropriate.
Players must not add extra approach steps.
coachingPoints: Focus on one coaching point at a time.
Keep the step short and balanced.
Maintain the head over the ball.
Use a compact but complete leg swing.
Guide the football directly onto the boot.
The drill should not become a rushed stab kick.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the kick becomes short and stabbing.
regressions: Rehearse the preparation and step without kicking.
matchApplication:
One-step kicks are required when players have limited space after:
A ground-ball gather.
A handball receive.
A stoppage release.
A mark close to pressure.
Turning away from an opponent.

title: Boundary-Line Kick
primarySkill: Kicking from a Restricted Boundary Position
objective: Develop the ability to kick effectively when the boundary line limits the player’s available movement and passing angle. Players learn to protect the football, open the body and select a safe target without stepping out of bounds.
players: Minimum: 6 Ideal: 10–18 Maximum: 24 using multiple groups
setup:
Use a painted boundary line or create one with cones.
Place the kicker approximately one metre inside the boundary.
Position three receiving targets:
One short and inside.
One longer along the boundary.
One central target at a wider angle.
A feeder stands behind or inside the kicker.
Players form lines at all positions.
howTheDrillWorks:
The feeder passes the football to the kicker near the boundary.
The kicker scans the available targets.
The coach may nominate one target as unavailable.
The kicker adjusts body position without crossing the boundary.
The kicker selects and delivers to the best available target.
The receiver marks or gathers the football.
Players rotate positions.
Repeat from both sides of the ground.
Players should practise kicking from both left and right boundaries.
coachingPoints: Focus on one coaching point at a time.
Keep the football protected on the inside.
Open the hips towards the selected target.
Use an appropriate kick for the angle.
The boundary should influence the decision but not create panic.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether players repeatedly choose the same option.
Use clear cones if players cannot see the boundary.
progressions: Reduce available space near the boundary.
Add a kick around the mark.
regressions: Tell the player which option to use.
Allow the player to begin stationary with the football.
successIndicators: Deliver accurate kicks from both boundaries.
matchApplication:
Boundary-line kicking occurs during:
General play.
Marks near the line.
Defensive exits.
Wing possession.
Forward-pocket entries.
Kicks after boundary-side ground balls.

title: Quick Release Kick
objective: Develop the ability to receive possession and execute an accurate kick with minimal delay. Players learn to scan before receiving, prepare the football immediately and complete the disposal before nearby pressure can arrive.
players: Minimum: 6 Ideal: 10–18 Maximum: 24 using multiple groups
setup:
Create three positions:
Feeder.
Central receiver.
Two final targets.
Place the feeder approximately 10–15 metres from the central receiver.
Place the final targets approximately 15–25 metres beyond the receiver, one to the left and one to the right.
Players form lines at each position.
howTheDrillWorks:
The receiver scans both final targets.
The feeder passes the football to the receiver.
As the football travels, the coach calls either “left” or “right.”
The receiver secures possession.
The receiver prepares the football immediately.
The receiver takes no more than one or two steps.
The receiver kicks to the nominated target.
Players rotate through each position.
Continue for the allocated time.
The coach may progressively delay the directional call to increase difficulty.
coachingPoints: Focus on one coaching point at a time.
Move it immediately into kicking position.
Use one balanced step where possible.
Maintain accuracy despite the reduced time.
Players should become quicker through preparation rather than through rushed technique.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether players rush the ball drop.
Whether the time pressure is appropriate.
Increase the available time if technical quality repeatedly collapses.
progressions: Require non-preferred foot use for one side.
Begin with a ground ball or handball receive.
regressions: Call the target before the feed.
Allow the receiver to begin with the football.
successIndicators: Deliver accurate kicks to both sides.
matchApplication:
Quick release kicks are required when players receive near pressure during:
Stoppage exits.
Forward-half turnovers.
Defensive rebounds.
Handball chains.
Short marks followed by immediate play-on.

title: Kick Around the Mark
primarySkill: Kicking Around a Player on the Mark
objective: Develop the ability to create a clear kicking lane around a player standing the mark. Players learn to move laterally with control, maintain balance and deliver accurately without drifting excessively or crossing the mark.
players: Minimum: 6 Ideal: 10–18 Maximum: 24 using multiple groups
equipment: Bibs for players on the mark.
setup:
Place one kicking cone and one mark cone approximately five metres apart.
Position two receiving targets 20–30 metres away:
One to the left.
One to the right.
A player stands on the mark cone.
The kicker begins behind the kicking cone with the football.
howTheDrillWorks:
The kicker scans both target options.
The player on the mark holds position with arms raised.
The kicker moves laterally to either side.
The kicker creates a clear lane around the mark.
The kicker balances and delivers to the selected target.
The receiver marks or gathers the football.
Players rotate through kicker, mark and receiver roles.
Continue from both sides.
The player on the mark may initially remain stationary before introducing controlled lateral movement.
coachingPoints: Focus on one coaching point at a time.
Align the hips and shoulders with the target.
Avoid leaning backwards while moving sideways.
Complete the kick before the mark closes the angle.
Players should not run so far sideways that the kick becomes unnecessarily difficult.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the player on the mark remains controlled.
Encourage players to practise moving both left and right.
progressions: Allow the player on the mark to move laterally.
Reduce the distance between kicker and mark.
Require the non-preferred foot on one side.
Add a second defender closing from behind.
regressions: Use a stationary pole instead of a player.
Increase the starting distance from the mark.
Tell the kicker which side to use.
Allow the kicker to stop completely before kicking.
successIndicators: Deliver accurate kicks to both sides.
matchApplication:
Players regularly need to kick around the mark after:
Taking a mark.
Receiving a free kick.
Playing near the boundary.
Switching direction.
Attempting a short-angle pass.

title: Mark, Play On and Kick
objective: Develop the ability to mark the football, recognise available space and play on quickly before executing an accurate kick. Players learn to prepare the next action before the mark is completed.
players: Minimum: 6 Ideal: 9–18 Maximum: 24 using multiple groups
setup:
Create three positions:
Feeder.
Marking player.
Final target.
Place the feeder and marking player approximately 15 metres apart.
Place two play-on gates, one left and one right of the marking player.
Place the final target 20–30 metres beyond the gates.
Players form lines at all three positions.
howTheDrillWorks:
The marking player scans both play-on gates.
The feeder kicks to the marking player.
The player marks the football.
The coach calls “left” or “right.”
The player plays on through the nominated gate.
The player accelerates for several steps.
The player kicks to the final target.
Players rotate through each position.
Continue for the allocated time.
The directional call may be made before or immediately after the mark depending on the group’s ability.
coachingPoints: Focus on one coaching point at a time.
Turn quickly towards the selected gate.
The player should not play on automatically if the space is unavailable in a match. The drill teaches execution when the opportunity exists.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether players drift outside the gate.
progressions: Add a player on the mark.
Require non-preferred foot use on one side.
Allow the player to choose whether to play on.
regressions: Call the direction before the kick arrives.
Allow the player to walk through the pattern.
Begin with a handball feed instead of a kick.
successIndicators: Complete the sequence without unnecessary delay.
matchApplication:
Mark-and-play-on situations occur when players:
Take an uncontested mark.
Recognise open space.
Move the ball quickly through defence.
Attack through the corridor.
Create a fast forward entry.

title: Side-Step from the Mark
objective: Develop the ability to use a controlled side-step to move around a player on the mark before executing an accurate kick. Players learn to shift the defender, protect the football and regain alignment quickly.
players: Minimum: 6 Ideal: 10–18 Maximum: 24 using multiple groups
equipment: Bibs for players on the mark.
setup:
Place one kicker behind a mark cone.
Position a player on the mark approximately five metres away.
Place two receiving targets 20–25 metres beyond the mark, one left and one right.
The kicker begins with the football.
Players form lines at all positions.
howTheDrillWorks:
The kicker approaches the mark under control.
The kicker uses a small side-step or body feint.
The player on the mark reacts but does not tackle.
The kicker moves into the created lane.
The kicker regains balance.
The kicker delivers to one of the two targets.
Players rotate positions.
Practise side-stepping in both directions.
The kicker should avoid running too close to the mark.
coachingPoints: Focus on one coaching point at a time.
Use the hips, shoulders and eyes to sell the feint.
Take a decisive step into the new lane.
The side-step should create a disposal lane, not simply evade for its own sake.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Keep the mark passive until players demonstrate safe control.
progressions: Allow the mark to apply controlled contact.
regressions: Replace the player with a pole.
Tell the kicker which direction to step.
Allow the player to stop before kicking.
successIndicators: Move the mark with the feint.
Perform the movement in both directions.
matchApplication:
Side-stepping the mark can create:
A clearer kicking lane.
A better angle inside 50.
Space to use the non-preferred side.
A corridor option.
Time to avoid a smother.

title: Short Mark and Switch Kick
objective: Develop the ability to mark the football, scan across the ground and switch play to a target positioned away from the original direction of the pass.
players: Minimum: 7 Ideal: 10–18 Maximum: 24 using multiple groups
setup:
Create three positions in an angled pattern:
Feeder.
Central marking player.
Switch target positioned 20–30 metres to the opposite side.
Place an optional second target directly ahead to create a visual alternative.
Players form lines at each position.
howTheDrillWorks:
The central player scans towards the switch target.
The feeder kicks to the central player.
The central player marks the football.
The player turns away from the direction of the original pass.
The player balances and kicks to the switch target.
The switch target marks the football.
Players rotate through all positions.
Reverse the direction after several minutes.
The coach may occasionally call for the direct target to keep players scanning both options.
coachingPoints: Focus on one coaching point at a time.
Mark with the body prepared to turn.
Secure the football before changing direction.
Open the hips towards the switch target.
The switch should move the football into space rather than simply sideways.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether players automatically kick straight ahead.
progressions: Add a player on the mark.
Allow the player to choose between direct and switch options.
